Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?\n\nPatient: I keep seeing that explosion in my head like it’s happening all over again, and I can’t shut it off. It just plays over and over, and I can't get away from it.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been experiencing these recurring memories of the explosion, and did they start right after the event happened?\n\nPatient: I’ve been dealing with these memories for about 14 months now, ever since the explosion happened. They started pretty much right after the accident, and instead of fading over time, they've just dug in and become a constant part of my daily life.\n\nDoctor: Have you been avoiding people, places, or activities that remind you of the explosion, or is there anything you used to enjoy that you've stopped doing because of these memories?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I take the long way around just to avoid older buildings and that side of town, and I walk away if anyone at church brings up the accident. I've also stopped playing basketball with the guys and helping with the youth program because none of it feels fun anymore.\n\nDoctor: Do you often!!!!!find yourself being easily startled or having difficulty falling or staying asleep due to constantly being on the lookout for potential dangers?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. If someone drops a tool on the job or slams a car door, I jump out of my skin and my heart starts pounding like crazy. Sleep is just as bad—I lie awake until two or three in the morning, only to jerk awake sweating from nightmares of the fire and feeling too wired to rest.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a recent situation where you felt extremely on edge or had a strong startle response, and how you reacted to it?\n\nPatient: Just the other day at work, one of the guys dropped a heavy pipe wrench on the concrete right behind me. I jumped completely out of my skin, my heart started hammering in my chest, and I couldn't stop shaking for a long time even after I realized it was just a tool.\n\nDoctor: Have you been experiencing significant difficulty concentrating on tasks or activities due to being constantly on the lookout for potential dangers or threats?\n\nPatient: I can't say I've noticed having a hard time concentrating just from looking out for danger. But I definitely feel tense and on edge pretty much all the time, like my body is constantly waiting for something bad to happen.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your mood, such as feeling hopeless, guilty, or persistently irritable, since the explosion happened?\n\nPatient: Yes, I walk around most days with this heavy mix of dread and anger in my chest, always waiting for something bad to happen. I also carry this deep guilt and honestly hate myself because I got to walk away from that blast while my young apprentice died.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about the guilt you're feeling, specifically what thoughts or memories trigger these feelings of guilt and self-hatred related to the explosion?\n\nPatient: I just can't stop thinking about how I got out of that basement with only minor burns while my young apprentice was severely hurt and died. I constantly ask myself why I was the one who got to live when he had his whole life ahead of him. It leaves me with this heavy dread and self-hatred that I just can't shake.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you had done something differently during the explosion, the outcome would have been different, and is that contributing to your feelings of guilt?\n\nPatient: I torment myself with \"what ifs\" all the time, but the most frustrating part is that I have this huge blank spot in my memory right when the blast hit and how we got out. Because I can't remember those exact minutes, I don't know what I did or didn't do, which just makes the guilt and self-hatred so much worse.\n\nDoctor: Have you been experiencing any physical symptoms like headaches or stomach problems when these memories or feelings of guilt come up, or is it more emotional distress that you're dealing with?\n\nPatient: I don't really get headaches or stomach aches, but I definitely feel a lot of physical symptoms alongside the emotional distress. My chest constantly feels heavy and tight with dread, my muscles are always tense, and my body feels wired and restless at night even when I'm exhausted. Plus, whenever I get startled, my heart pounds like crazy and I can't stop shaking.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned having a 'huge blank spot' in your memory right when the blast hit and how you got out, can you tell me more about what you mean by that and how often you experience these memory gaps?\n\nPatient: I remember going down those basement stairs and smelling the gas, but the next thing I know, I was waking up outside with people shouting. Everything in between—the actual blast and how I got out of there—is a complete blank that I just can't piece together. It's not like I'm forgetful in my daily life; it's just this one permanent, specific gap from the accident that is completely gone.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about this 'blank spot' in your memory, and have you experienced any other episodes where you felt disconnected from yourself or your surroundings since the explosion?\n\nPatient: Like I said, those minutes of the blast are just a complete blank in my mind that I can't recover. Aside from that, I often feel totally numb, like I'm disconnected and just watching someone else live my life. And when the flashbacks hit, I completely lose touch with where I am and feel like I'm right back in that burning basement.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how often you feel numb or disconnected from yourself and your surroundings, and does this feeling of disconnection happen only during the flashbacks or at other times as well?\n\nPatient: The numbness actually happens during normal, everyday moments, not just when I'm having a flashback. For example, when my little niece runs up to hug me or my crew finishes a job, I just feel totally blank inside, like I'm watching someone else's life and can't feel any real happiness or love. During the flashbacks, it's the opposite—I'm not numb, I'm completely pulled back into the actual terror of the explosion itself.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much of your daily life is affected by this feeling of being numb or disconnected from yourself and your surroundings, and are there any specific triggers that make you feel more or less disconnected?"

Because of this, I've ended up pulling away from my friends and family because I just can't connect or show up for them like I used to.

During the flashbacks, it's the opposite—I'm not numb, I'm completely pulled back into the actual terror of the explosion itself.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much of your daily life is affected by this feeling of being numb or disconnected from yourself and your surroundings, and are there any specific triggers that make you feel more or less disconnected?\n\nPatient: This numbness is pretty much a constant daily presence for me, making me feel like I'm just watching my own life from the outside. Sleep is just as bad—I lie awake until two or three in the morning, only to jerk awake sweating from nightmares of the fire and feeling too wired to rest.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a recent situation where you felt extremely on edge or had a strong startle response, and how you reacted to it?\n\nPatient: Just the other day at work, one of the guys dropped a heavy pipe wrench on the concrete right behind me. I jumped completely out of my skin, my heart started hammering in my chest, and I couldn't stop shaking for a long time even after I realized it was just a tool.\n\nDoctor: Have you been experiencing significant difficulty concentrating on tasks or activities due to being constantly on the lookout for potential dangers or threats?\n\nPatient: I can't say I've noticed having a hard time concentrating just from looking out for danger. But I definitely feel tense and on edge pretty much all the time, like my body is constantly waiting for something bad to happen.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your mood, such as feeling hopeless, guilty, or persistently irritable, since the explosion happened?\n\nPatient: Yes, I walk around most days with this heavy mix of dread and anger in my chest, always waiting for something bad to happen. I also carry this deep guilt and honestly hate myself because I got to walk away from that blast while my young apprentice died.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about the guilt you're feeling, specifically what thoughts or memories trigger these feelings of guilt and self-hatred related to the explosion?\n\nPatient: I just can't stop thinking about how I got out of that basement with only minor burns while my young apprentice was severely hurt and died. I constantly ask myself why I was the one who got to live when he had his whole life ahead of him. It leaves me with this heavy dread and self-hatred that I just can't shake.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you had done something differently during the explosion, the outcome would have been different, and is that contributing to your feelings of guilt?\n\nPatient: I torment myself with \"what ifs\" all the time, but the most frustrating part is that I have this huge blank spot in my memory right when the blast hit and how we got out. Because I can't remember those exact minutes, I don't know what I did or didn't do, which just makes the guilt and self-hatred so much worse.\n\nDoctor: Have you been experiencing any physical symptoms like headaches or stomach problems when these memories or feelings of guilt come up, or is it more emotional distress that you're dealing with?\n\nPatient: I don't really get headaches or stomach aches, but I definitely feel a lot of physical symptoms alongside the emotional distress. My chest constantly feels heavy and tight with dread, my muscles are always tense, and my body feels wired and restless at night even when I'm exhausted. Plus, whenever I get startled, my heart pounds like crazy and I can't stop shaking.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned having a 'huge blank spot' in your memory right when the blast hit and how you got out, can you tell me more about what you mean by that and how often you experience these memory gaps?\n\nPatient: I remember going down those basement stairs and smelling the gas, but the next thing I know, I was waking up outside with people shouting. Everything in between—the actual blast and how I got out of there—is a complete blank that I just can't piece together. It's not like I'm forgetful in my daily life; it's just this one permanent, specific gap from the accident that is completely gone.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about this 'blank spot' in your memory, and have you experienced any other episodes where you felt disconnected from yourself or your surroundings since the explosion?\n\nPatient: Like I said, those minutes of the blast are just a complete blank in my mind that I can't recover. Aside from that, I often feel totally numb, like I'm disconnected and just watching someone else live my life. And when the flashbacks hit, I completely lose touch with where I am and feel like I'm right back in that burning basement.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how often you feel numb or disconnected from yourself and your surroundings, and does this feeling of disconnection happen only during the flashbacks or at other times as well?\n\nPatient: The numbness actually happens during normal, everyday moments, not just when I'm having a flashback. For example, when my little niece runs up to hug me or my crew finishes a job, I just feel totally blank inside, like I'm watching someone else's life and can't feel any real happiness or love. During the flashbacks, it's the opposite—I'm not numb, I'm completely pulled back into the actual terror of the explosion itself.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much of your daily life is affected by this feeling of being numb or disconnected from yourself and your surroundings, and are there any specific triggers that make you feel more or less disconnected?\n\nPatient: This numbness is pretty much a constant daily presence for me, making me feel like I'm just watching my own life from the outside. It's most painful during moments that should be happy, like when my little niece hugs me or my work crew finishes a major job, but I feel absolutely nothing. Because of this, I've ended up pulling away from my friends and family because I just can't connect or show up for them like I used to.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how often you experience this feeling of being disconnected from yourself or your surroundings, is it happening several times a day, or is it more sporadic?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how to track it or put a specific number on how often it happens. It's just this heavy, constant feeling that is always there in the background, so it's hard to say if it's happening in separate episodes or if it's just one long stretch.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any recent situations where you felt like you were observing yourself from outside your body or felt like you were in a dream, and how often do these experiences occur?\n\nPatient: I don't really experience feeling like I'm outside of my body or in a dream. It is more that I just feel completely numb and flat emotionally, but I don't actually have those kinds of out-of-body experiences.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned feeling numb and disconnected from yourself and your surroundings, can you tell me if you've ever felt like you're living in a fog or that things around you seem unreal, and how often this happens?\n\nPatient: I don't really feel like I'm living in a fog or that the world around me is unreal. It's more that I just feel completely numb inside and disconnected from my own emotions. It feels like I'm just watching my life happen to someone else.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if you've ever felt like you're watching yourself from outside your body or like you're in a dream during these episodes of numbness and disconnection?"

During the flashbacks, it's the opposite—I'm not numb, I'm completely pulled back into the actual terror of the explosion itself.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much of your daily life is affected by this feeling of being numb or disconnected from yourself and your surroundings, and are there any specific triggers that make you feel more or less disconnected?\n\nPatient: This numbness is pretty much a constant daily presence for me, making me feel like I'm just watching my own life from the outside. It's most painful during moments that should be happy, like when my little niece hugs me or my work crew finishes a major job, but I feel absolutely nothing. Because of this, I've ended up pulling away from my friends and family because I just can't connect or show up for them like I used to.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how often you experience this feeling of being disconnected from yourself or your surroundings, is it happening several times a day, or is it more sporadic?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how to track it or put a specific number on how often it happens. It's more that I just feel completely numb inside and disconnected from my own emotions. It feels like I'm just watching my life happen to someone else.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if you've ever felt like you're watching yourself from outside your body or like you're in a dream during these episodes of numbness and disconnection?\n\nPatient: No, I don't literally float outside my body or feel like I'm in a dream. It's more that the numbness makes me feel like I'm just watching someone else's life play out instead of actually living my own. It is especially hard when I'm trying to connect with my loved ones, because I'm physically there but feel completely shut off from any real emotions.\n\nDoctor: You've described feeling numb and disconnected, can you tell me if there are any specific situations or triggers that make you feel more connected to yourself and your surroundings, or if there's anything that helps you feel more grounded in reality?\n\nPatient: To be honest, I haven't found anything that helps me feel grounded or connected right now. It leaves me with this heavy dread and self-hatred that I just can't shake.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you had done something differently during the explosion, the outcome would have been different, and is that contributing to your feelings of guilt?\n\nPatient: I torment myself with \"what ifs\" all the time, but the most frustrating part is that I have this huge blank spot in my memory right when the blast hit and how we got out. Because I can't remember those exact minutes, I don't know what I did or didn't do, which just makes the guilt and self-hatred so much worse.\n\nDoctor: Have you been experiencing any physical symptoms like headaches or stomach problems when these memories or feelings of guilt come up, or is it more emotional distress that you're dealing with?\n\nPatient: I don't really get headaches or stomach aches, but I definitely feel a lot of physical symptoms alongside the emotional distress. My chest constantly feels heavy and tight with dread, my muscles are always tense, and my body feels wired and restless at night even when I'm exhausted. Plus, whenever I get startled, my heart pounds like crazy and I can't stop shaking.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned having a 'huge blank spot' in your memory right when the blast hit and how you got out, can you tell me more about what you mean by that and how often you experience these memory gaps?\n\nPatient: I remember going down those basement stairs and smelling the gas, but the next thing I know, I was waking up outside with people shouting. Everything in between—the actual blast and how I got out of there—is a complete blank that I just can't piece together. It's not like I'm forgetful in my daily life; it's just this one permanent, specific gap from the accident that is completely gone.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about this 'blank spot' in your memory, and have you experienced any other episodes where you felt disconnected from yourself or your surroundings since the explosion?\n\nPatient: Like I said, those minutes of the blast are just a complete blank in my mind that I can't recover. Aside from that, I often feel totally numb, like I'm disconnected and just watching someone else live my life. And when the flashbacks hit, I completely lose touch with where I am and feel like I'm right back in that burning basement.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how often you feel numb or disconnected from yourself and your surroundings, and does this feeling of disconnection happen only during the flashbacks or at other times as well?\n\nPatient: The numbness actually happens during normal, everyday moments, not just when I'm having a flashback. For example, when my little niece runs up to hug me or my crew finishes a job, I just feel totally blank inside, like I'm watching someone else's life and can't feel any real happiness or love. During the flashbacks, it's the opposite—I'm not numb, I'm completely pulled back into the actual terror of the explosion itself.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much of your daily life is affected by this feeling of being numb or disconnected from yourself and your surroundings, and are there any specific triggers that make you feel more or less disconnected?\n\nPatient: This numbness is pretty much a constant daily presence for me, making me feel like I'm just watching my own life from the outside. It's most painful during moments that should be happy, like when my little niece hugs me or my work crew finishes a major job, but I feel absolutely nothing. Because of this, I've ended up pulling away from my friends and family because I just can't connect or show up for them like I used to.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how often you experience this feeling of being disconnected from yourself or your surroundings, is it happening several times a day, or is it more sporadic?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how to track it or put a specific number on how often it happens. It's just this heavy, constant feeling that is always there in the background, so it's hard to say if it's happening in separate episodes or if it's just one long stretch.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any recent situations where you felt like you were observing yourself from outside your body or felt like you were in a dream, and how often do these experiences occur?\n\nPatient: I don't really experience feeling like I'm outside of my body or in a dream. It is more that I just feel completely numb and flat emotionally, but I don't actually have those kinds of out-of-body experiences.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned feeling numb and disconnected from yourself and your surroundings, can you tell me if you've ever felt like you're living in a fog or that things around you seem unreal, and how often this happens?\n\nPatient: I don't really feel like I'm living in a fog or that the world around me is unreal. It's more that I just feel completely numb inside and disconnected from my own emotions. It feels like I'm just watching my life happen to someone else.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if you've ever felt like you're watching yourself from outside your body or like you're in a dream during these episodes of numbness and disconnection?\n\nPatient: No, I don't literally float outside my body or feel like I'm in a dream. It's more that the numbness makes me feel like I'm just watching someone else's life play out instead of actually living my own. It is especially hard when I'm trying to connect with my loved ones, because I'm physically there but feel completely shut off from any real emotions.\n\nDoctor: You've described feeling numb and disconnected, can you tell me if there are any specific situations or triggers that make you feel more connected to yourself and your surroundings, or if there's anything that helps you feel more grounded in reality?\n\nPatient: To be honest, I haven't found anything that helps me feel grounded or connected right now. Everything in my life just feels completely numb, distant, and out of reach. I haven't come across any situation or coping mechanism that actually makes me feel present.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if the feeling of numbness and disconnection you experience is more related to the traumatic event itself or if it's a general feeling that pervades most aspects of your life, including times when you're not thinking about the explosion?\n\nPatient: It’s definitely a general, constant feeling that hangs over my entire life, even during moments completely unrelated to the explosion. For instance, when my little niece runs up to hug me or we finish a big job at work, I just feel completely blank and disconnected, like I’m watching someone else’s life without being able to feel any real happiness or love.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned feeling numb and disconnected from your emotions and life, can you tell me if this feeling of numbness is something that you experience only in response to reminders of the explosion or if it's a more pervasive feeling that affects your daily life and relationships regardless of the context?"
  }
